root_idea.summary: The root centers on aversion: hating, finding something odious, and withdrawing from it.
root_idea.development: The core sense develops from abhorrence and avoidance into hatred, hostility, and descriptions of persons who hate or are hated; a related branch denotes scrupulous withdrawal from impurity.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Displayed under the normalized active-participle citation form شَانِئٌ.
Displayed as the noun شَنَآنٌ, the citation form corresponding to the Quranic inflected occurrences.

senses.definition: One who hates; an enemy or hostile detractor.
senses.usage_conditions: An active-participle noun referring to the person characterized by hatred, as in the Quranic construction شَانِئُكَ / شَانِئَكَ, “your hater” or “your enemy.”

senses.definition: Hatred or hostile aversion, especially hatred directed toward a people.
senses.usage_conditions: Used in the Quranic construction شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ, where the hatred of a people is presented as an attitude that may affect conduct. The supplied Quran occurrences are 5:2 and 5:8.
A reported Quranic reading or grammatical analysis treats the form associated with شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ as an epithet meaning “hateful” or “odious,” rather than as the verbal noun “hatred.”

other_classical_meanings.definition: To hate, or to hate vehemently; in the passive, to be hated or rendered hateful.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verb has several transmitted infinitive forms. The passive description may apply even to someone otherwise beautiful or comely.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To acknowledge and deliver a person’s right or due; to produce what is owed and thereby clear oneself of the matter.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used in constructions with لَهُ, إِلَيْهِ, or بِهِ; the transmitted explanations combine acknowledgment, payment or production, and discharge from an obligation.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To hate one another; to be mutually hostile.
Hatred, especially vehement hatred or hatred mixed with enmity and bad disposition.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The lexical discussion lists شَنْءٌ, شِنْءٌ, شُنْءٌ and related infinitival or nominal variants as forms used for this meaning.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A hateful or odious person, or someone evil in disposition.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used as an epithet for a man, describing him as rendered hateful or as an object of hatred, even if other qualities make him loved.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Scrupulous withdrawal or keeping oneself far from unclean things; continual purification. It can also describe a person who practices such abstinence.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The word is used both as a substantive and as an epithet for one who keeps aloof from impurity. The related form شُنُوءَةٌ is also reported.
A reported interpretation, especially in an explanation of the tribal name Azd Shanu'a; this is distinct from the better-known sense of withdrawal from impurity.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Pure lineage together with manly virtue and good conduct.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reported use connected with the phrase رجل شَنُوءَةٍ and with an alternative explanation of the tribal name.

other_classical_meanings.definition: What is regarded as sordid or contemptible in words and actions.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A rare reported use attributed through a secondary citation in the lexical tradition.

other_classical_meanings.definition: An epithet for a man who hates, or who is hated or odious.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The transmitted authorities differ over whether the epithet denotes the hater or the hated person; the feminine forms شَنْآنَةٌ and شَنْأَى are also reported.

other_classical_meanings.definition: In a metaphorical expression, the cold of winter; alternatively, ease and repose.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The expression is explained through the idea that winter cold is hated, while another interpretation takes the intended meaning to be mutual hatred or, figuratively, ease and repose.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Literally, “may there be no father to your hater”; idiomatically, an expression of praise equivalent to لَا أَبَا لَكَ.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A conventional metonymical expression; شَانِئِكَ here means “your hater.”

other_classical_meanings.definition: Livestock or property freely given away rather than grudgingly retained.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: In this expression the plural active participle is used with passive force, as though the property were hated and therefore liberally relinquished.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Foul or ugly in appearance, especially in the face.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An epithet that may apply even when the person is made an object of love by good qualities; the form is reported as usable across number and gender.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who hates people, one whom people hate, or one who does much for which hatred is incurred.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: These are alternative transmitted explanations of the intensive form; the evidence does not reduce them to a single direction of the hatred relation.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Hated, rendered hateful, or made an object of hatred.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An adjectival passive description that may apply even to someone beautiful or comely; the variants مَشْنُوٌّ and مَشْنِىٌّ are reported with the same sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A kind of liquid or soft food, such as broth or porridge, taken by sipping or spooning.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A technical culinary use occurring in a transmitted report; its irregular morphological derivation does not establish that the food itself means “hated.”

cautions: The Quranic form شَنَآنٌ has a reported alternative reading or grammatical analysis as an adjective meaning “hateful” or “odious”; the standard QAC form is presented separately from that reported interpretation.
Lane’s Quran references in the lexical discussion use historical citation notation and are not converted into modern verse locations unless independently supplied by QAC.
